title: Valid Sudoku
description: Brute force to optimized: separately re-scanning rows, columns, and boxes versus a single pass tracking all three overlapping groupings simultaneously.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given a 9x9 Sudoku board (partially filled), determine if it is valid according to Sudoku rules: only the FILLED cells (digits '1'-'9') need to be validated, and each row, each column, and each of the nine 3x3 sub-boxes must contain no repeated digit. Empty cells are represented by '.' and can be ignored.

blocks.caption: Track seen digits per row, per column, and per 3x3 box, all in a single pass

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A cell participates in THREE overlapping groups: its row, its column, and its 3x3 box","Track seen digits for all three groups simultaneously, checked together for every cell"],["Only need to detect a DUPLICATE, not validate a complete solution","A hash set per group, checked before insertion, catches a duplicate the instant it appears"],["A cell's (row, column) position determines its box deterministically","A simple index formula, (row // 3) * 3 + (column // 3), maps any cell to its box number 0-8"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a 9x9 grid with some cells filled with digits and others empty, check whether every row, column, and 3x3 box contains no repeated digit among its filled cells.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking Three Overlapping Attendance Sheets at Once
blocks.text: Like checking that no person's name appears twice on any of three overlapping attendance sheets they could belong to (their row's sheet, their column's sheet, and their local group's sheet), all while walking through the room just once. For each person encountered, checking all three of their relevant sheets and marking their name off on all three simultaneously catches any duplicate the moment it happens, without ever needing to re-check any sheet from scratch.

blocks.caption: Every cell is checked against and marked into its row, column, and box sets together

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?
Before separately re-scanning every row, then every column, then every box (each from scratch), notice that a single pass over every cell can check and update all three relevant groups at once.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every filled cell belongs to exactly 3 groups that must each avoid duplicates: its row, its column, and its 3x3 box.

Observation 2: A cell at (i, j) belongs to box number (i // 3) * 3 + (j // 3), a simple, direct formula requiring no lookup or search.

Observation 3: Maintaining a hash set per row, per column, and per box (27 sets total, for a 9x9 board), a single pass over every cell can check whether its digit already exists in any of its 3 relevant sets; if so, a duplicate has been found and the board is invalid immediately.

Observation 4: If the digit doesn't already exist in any of its 3 relevant sets, add it to all 3, then continue to the next cell.

Recognizing that checking and updating all 3 overlapping groups together, in one single pass, avoids ever needing separate re-scans of the whole board for rows, then columns, then boxes.
This is a direct hash-set tracking pattern, generalized to three simultaneous, overlapping groupings (row, column, box) instead of just one, with a simple index formula determining box membership.
6. Brute Force Solution
Separately re-scan every row, then every column, then every 3x3 box, checking each for duplicates independently.
Step by step algorithm

items: Check every row for duplicate digits among its filled cells.
Check every column for duplicate digits among its filled cells.
Check every 3x3 box for duplicate digits among its filled cells.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Each grouping (rows, then columns, then boxes) is checked completely independently, since this brute force does not yet combine the three checks into a single pass.
A helper function checks a single group for duplicates by counting non-empty digits against the size of their deduplicated set.
The board is scanned three separate times overall (once per grouping type), fully re-reading every cell each time.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every row, column, and box is checked independently and completely, so any duplicate is always correctly detected.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), since a 9x9 board has a fixed size, though conceptually this scans the board 3 times (once per grouping type) rather than once; for a general N x N board this would be O(N squared).
Space: O(1) for a fixed 9x9 board (O(N) generally, for the temporary group arrays).

Limitation: scanning the board three separate times (once per grouping type) does more work than necessary, when a single pass could check and update all three relevant groupings for each cell simultaneously.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force scans the board three separate times. Instead, maintain 27 hash sets total: one per row, one per column, and one per 3x3 box. In a single pass over every cell, compute its box index directly via (row // 3) * 3 + (column // 3), then check its digit against all three relevant sets at once; if found in any, the board is invalid. Otherwise, add the digit to all three sets and continue.

Initialize 9 row sets, 9 column sets, and 9 box sets, all empty. In a single pass over every (i, j) cell, skip empty cells; for filled cells, compute the box index, check the digit against rows[i], cols[j], and boxes[boxIdx]; if a match is found in any, return false immediately. Otherwise add the digit to all three, and continue. Return true if the entire board is processed with no duplicates found.
9. Optimized Solution
Track seen digits per row, column, and box simultaneously, checking and updating all three for every filled cell in a single pass.

blocks.title: Continuing across the full board
blocks.text: The same check-and-mark process continues for every remaining cell; since the full example board has no duplicates in any row, column, or box, the final result is true.

codes.python:
def is_valid_sudoku(board):
    rows = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    cols = [set() for _ in range(9)]
    boxes = [set() for _ in range(9)]                                       # one set per 3x3 box, indexed 0-8 in row-major box order
    for i in range(9):
        for j in range(9):
            c = board[i][j]
            if c == '.':
                continue
            box_idx = (i // 3) * 3 + (j // 3)                               # maps any (i,j) to its containing box's index, 0-8
            if c in rows[i] or c in cols[j] or c in boxes[box_idx]:
                return False                                                # this digit already appeared in its row, column, or box
            rows[i].add(c)
            cols[j].add(c)
            boxes[box_idx].add(c)
    return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    board = [
        list('53..7....'),
        list('6..195...'),
        list('.98....6.'),
        list('8...6...3'),
        list('4..8.3..1'),
        list('7...2...6'),
        list('.6....28.'),
        list('...419..5'),
        list('....8..79'),
    ]
    print(is_valid_sudoku(board))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for a fixed 9x9 board (a single pass over all 81 cells; generally O(N squared) for an N x N board).
Space: O(1) for a fixed board size (27 sets of at most 9 digits each; generally O(N) per set).
Why This Works

Every filled cell belongs to exactly one row, one column, and one box, and the box index formula (i // 3) * 3 + (j // 3) computes that membership directly with no search needed. Checking a digit against all three relevant sets before inserting it catches a duplicate the instant it would occur in ANY of the three groupings, and inserting into all three keeps every set correctly up to date for future cells.

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The box index formula (i / 3) * 3 + (j / 3) relies on integer division, correctly grouping the 9x9 board into nine 3x3 blocks numbered 0-8 in row-major order.
The three-way check (rows[i], cols[j], boxes[boxIdx]) happens BEFORE any insertion, ensuring a cell is never counted as a duplicate of itself.
A single nested loop over all 81 cells replaces the brute force's three separate full-board scans.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

When a single element belongs to multiple overlapping validation groups (here, row, column, and box), tracking all of them simultaneously in one pass avoids redundant full re-scans of the same data structure for each grouping type separately.
Common mistakes

items: Getting the box index formula wrong (e.g., using i * 3 + j instead of (i // 3) * 3 + (j // 3)), which would incorrectly group cells that aren't actually in the same 3x3 block.
Forgetting to skip empty ('.') cells, which would incorrectly try to validate non-digit placeholders.
Checking for duplicates AFTER inserting instead of before, which would incorrectly always report a duplicate (since the digit would already have just been added to its own set).

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: State the box index formula explicitly and explain why it works (integer division groups any (i,j) into one of 9 non-overlapping 3x3 regions), since this specific piece of arithmetic is often the part interviewers watch most closely for correctness.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Validate a grid where cells belong to multiple overlapping groups (rows, columns, sub-regions)" points toward tracking a hash set per group for every group type, checked and updated together in a single pass.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you use bitmasks instead of hash sets for a small, fixed digit range like 1-9? A 9-bit integer per row/column/box, with bitwise checks and OR-updates, replaces hash sets with faster, more memory-efficient bit manipulation.

How would this generalize to a different sub-grid size (e.g., a 16x16 Sudoku variant with 4x4 boxes)? The box index formula generalizes directly: (i // boxSize) * numBoxesPerRow + (j // boxSize), with numBoxesPerRow being the grid width divided by boxSize.

How would you extend this to also SOLVE a Sudoku puzzle, not just validate one? That becomes a substantially different backtracking search problem, though the same row/column/box tracking sets remain useful for quickly checking candidate placements during the search.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A hash-set-based duplicate detection pattern, generalized to multiple simultaneous overlapping groupings, distinct from Toeplitz Matrix's single-diagonal-grouping check elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) time (3 scans) for fixed 9x9, O(1) space.
Optimized (single pass, 3 simultaneous checks): O(1) time (1 scan) for fixed 9x9, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Hash-set duplicate tracking across multiple simultaneous, overlapping groupings (row, column, and box)
Core Idea: Every cell belongs to exactly one row, column, and box; checking and marking all three together in a single pass avoids redundant re-scans
Time: O(1) for a fixed 9x9 board (a single full pass)
Space: O(1) for a fixed 9x9 board
Most Important Observation: A cell's box membership is computed directly via (row // 3) * 3 + (column // 3), requiring no search
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Check rows[i], cols[j], boxes[(i/3)*3+(j/3)] together before marking each digit as seen
